title: The Case for PowerPoint
author: Tom Lynch
summary: Tom Lynch pushes back on the fashionable view that teachers should abandon PowerPoint for visualisers and OneNote, arguing that his best lessons are still built around a slide deck. He questions the anecdotal evidence for the alternatives by noting that teachers who switch are probably more pedagogically engaged to begin with and often work in schools whose tight routines make almost any approach look effective. His central principle is that his decision-making is far better before a lesson than during it, because sequencing questions, images, prompts and worked examples takes time and mental clarity that a live lesson does not offer. He walks through a science lesson on electron energy levels to show how deliberately ordered slides and a pre-planned check for understanding let him spot a misconception and repair it. He answers critics by showing how blank slides, the see-all-slides view and pressing 'b' keep a deck flexible, and he insists the real divide is not PowerPoint equals bad teacher and visualiser equals good teacher.
points: Lynch argues the evidence for visualisers and OneNote is confounded, since teachers who switch tend to be more engaged and may work in schools with unusually strong routines.
His main principle is that teachers decide better before a lesson than during it, so sequencing questions, images, prompts and examples in advance protects against on-the-spot mistakes.
Complex question sequences are better displayed than spoken, because oral delivery overloads working memory, much as a pub quiz question must often be repeated.

A pre-planned deck can still be responsive: blank slides, the see-all-slides button and the 'b' blackout let a teacher pause, jump back or shift attention, as when he addressed a misconception before re-asking the question.
He urges leaders to model slide design that is minimal and intentional, and not an information-heavy lecture, and wants to dispel the idea that PowerPoint means a bad teacher.
quotes: Teachers who have made the switch to visualisers/OneNote are likely to be more pedagogically engaged, thus their lessons are superior for a whole range of other reasons. The teacher who clocked out of caring about what makes a good lesson is unlikely to have made the switch.

In many peoples arguments against PowerPoint, they suggest that a predetermined slide deck is too rigid to be responsive in class and that working from a ‘blank canvas’ enables you so adapt as you go. I think this is ignoring the fact the most classes are so incredibly predictable (‘oh yeah, pupils always get that question wrong’) that the point becomes almost redundant.

These are not trivial matters - how you craft and sequence the atoms of a lesson greatly impacts a students ability to ‘follow along’ with the intended learning. Deciding this on the spot mid-lesson requires incredible presence of mind which can be difficult to achieve with all else going on.

How many times during a pub quiz have you had to ask them to repeat the question? Holding a list of world landmarks in your head takes up the precious cognitive bandwidth required to estimate which of them is furthest from London as the crow flies.

Often my powerpoints are 30 or 40 slides long, with minimal content and small, intentional variation from one slide to the next. Designing this learning journey is, to me, the essence of being a teacher.
Most PowerPoint critics deem teachers capable of changing their entire working practice to embrace new technology, yet entirely incapable of editing some slides.

The pre-planned timeline that PowerPoint offers is part of the reason I like it so much. When I’ve acted in a more ‘off the cuff’ fashion in the past, I’ve often delivered two very different lessons to two classes.
